Editorial Examines Artificial Intelligence and Digital Tools in Modern Diabetes Management

In an editorial published in BMC Digital Health, researchers Rhiannon E. Hawkes and Lizheng Shi outline the growing role of digital health technologies and artificial intelligence in transforming diabetes care. The authors note that diabetes represents a major global health challenge affecting more than one in ten adults worldwide, with global economic costs projected to exceed 2.1 trillion dollars by 2030. Characterised by elevated blood glucose levels, the condition can lead to severe complications including loss of vision, nerve pain, limb amputation, and cardiovascular problems.

Traditional methods of diabetes monitoring have long relied on patient self-monitoring of blood glucose levels through regular finger-prick testing, manual record-keeping, and scheduled in-person consultations with clinicians. However, the authors emphasize that these conventional approaches carry significant practical limitations, as finger-prick testing offers only isolated snapshots of glucose levels rather than continuous daily trends. Frequent testing also presents notable inconvenience for patients and carries an increased risk of inaccurate readings, underscoring the ongoing operational pressure on healthcare systems, clinicians, and individuals living with diabetes.

Over the past decade, a rapid expansion in digital health technologies has introduced continuous real-time data collection, automated feedback, and remote communication pathways between patients and healthcare providers. For chronic conditions such as diabetes, where ongoing self-management and prompt therapeutic adjustments are vital for maintaining glycaemic control, digital innovations offer proactive and personalised alternatives. Technologies such as continuous glucose monitoring systems, smart insulin pens, and mobile health applications provide data-driven insights that assist patients in understanding their condition and actively managing daily care.

Mobile health interventions, including dedicated smartphone applications and short message service communications, incorporate diverse features to support diabetes self-management. These tools enable users to monitor health behaviours such as logging glucose measurements, meals, and physical activity, alongside access to structured educational content, online peer networks, behaviour change techniques, and targeted adherence prompts. The editorial highlights systematic review evidence demonstrating that mobile health interventions can improve both glycaemic control and patient self-efficacy, particularly when coupled with clinician feedback or clinical decision-support tools.

Structured education remains foundational to effective chronic care through diabetes self-management education and support services, which deliver targeted guidance on nutrition, physical activity, glucose tracking, and medication management. Transitioning these structured programmes into digital formats addresses key logistical barriers associated with traditional face-to-face sessions, such as travel requirements and childcare obligations. Research cited in the editorial confirms that digital education programmes are acceptable, clinically effective, and capable of fostering greater patient autonomy in daily self-care routines.

Despite the documented advantages of mobile interventions and digital education programmes, patient disengagement presents a critical bottleneck that can limit health benefits. The authors observe that when individuals cease interacting with digital tools, they miss vital intervention components necessary for optimal self-management, potentially leading to poorer health outcomes. Consequently, further empirical research is needed to determine which specific tool components users engage with or abandon, the volume of clinician support necessary to sustain engagement, and whether such assistance is most effectively delivered via telephone calls or messaging platforms.

Another major technological milestone highlighted by the authors is the expanding clinical adoption of continuous glucose monitors. As wearable medical devices, these monitors provide real-time glucose measurements, dynamic trend trajectories, and predictive alerts that offer a far more comprehensive view of glycaemic variability than intermittent finger-prick tests. However, uptake remains constrained by financial barriers, including inconsistent insurance reimbursement, such as Medicaid coverage gaps in the United States and funding restrictions within the National Health Service in the United Kingdom for adults with type 2 diabetes. In contrast, evidence from Australia indicates that a nationally subsidised monitoring programme proved cost-effective compared to self-funded models.

Beyond financial constraints, the editorial identifies several non-cost impediments that hinder the equitable integration of digital diabetes tools into routine practice. Key operational hurdles include poor alignment with existing clinical workflows, inadequate broadband connectivity in underserved regions, and patient reluctance to share personal health data due to absent data governance frameworks. Hawkes and Shi stress that developers and healthcare systems must construct digital tools that are transparent, accessible, and secure, ensuring they integrate seamlessly into clinical services and sustainable reimbursement mechanisms.

Ensuring equitable access across diverse patient populations requires targeted, patient-centred implementation strategies. Digital tools must be tailored to meet the needs of diverse user communities, particularly individuals with limited digital literacy or those residing in historically underserved areas. By designing digital diabetes solutions that are trustworthy and motivating, healthcare stakeholders can begin to mitigate systemic adoption barriers and prevent the widening of existing digital health divides.

Looking toward future developments, the authors emphasize the integration of artificial intelligence into wearable continuous monitors and virtual health chatbots, which aim to enhance care quality, lower costs, and assist clinicians in clinical decision-making. The editorial identifies an ongoing paradigm shift toward agentic digital health technologies, moving away from passive, rule-based systems toward proactive, intelligent platforms capable of autonomous reasoning, planning, and task execution. Through an upcoming journal collection in BMC Digital Health, Hawkes and Shi seek to foster interdisciplinary research across clinical, technological, and behavioural disciplines to optimize the real-world adoption, effectiveness, and equity of digital diabetes management.

Subject of Research: Digital health technologies, continuous glucose monitoring, and artificial intelligence in diabetes management

Article Title: Harnessing the potential for digital diabetes management in the era of artificial intelligence

Article References: Hawkes, R. E., & Shi, L. (2026). Harnessing the potential for digital diabetes management in the era of artificial intelligence. BMC Digital Health, 4(1), Article 46. https://doi.org/10.1186/s44247-026-00279-4

Keywords: diabetes management, digital health technologies, continuous glucose monitoring, artificial intelligence, glycaemic control, mobile health applications, diabetes self-management education, patient engagement, health behaviour change, wearable medical devices, smart insulin pens, digital divide, chronic disease care, health disparities, agentic artificial intelligence, remote patient monitoring
